note: Extracted from three practitioner sources held by this index: SRC-002 (LaValle et al., Peptide Handbook, 2022), SRC-003 (Campbell, Optimize Your Health with Therapeutic Peptides, 2023) and SRC-005 (Hack Smith, The Complete Guide to Peptides, 2025). BPC-157 is the deliberately harder half of this pair. There is no approved product, no human trial in anything held here, and three sources that describe three different regimens. The architecture's job on this record is to keep all of that visible at once without letting volume of discussion read as weight of evidence.

compound.shortDescription: A synthetic fifteen-amino-acid peptide, described by the sources held here as derived from a protein found in human gastric juice, with an extensive laboratory literature and — in anything this index holds — no human trial evidence at all.
compound.simpleSummary:
BPC-157 is a short synthetic peptide. The sources held here describe it as a fragment of a larger protein found in stomach fluid, which is where the name comes from: body protection compound.

It is discussed more than almost any other compound in this field, largely in the context of healing — tendons, ligaments, muscle, gut lining, skin. The sources held here report a considerable body of laboratory work behind those claims, and they are careful about how they say it: one describes the effects as observed "in laboratory studies", another as seen "in several animal studies, and even more anecdotal testimonials".

That wording is the most important thing on this page. Laboratory and animal work can show that something is worth studying in people. It cannot show that it works in people, and this index holds no study in people for BPC-157 — none. Not a small trial, not a poor trial. None.

The second thing worth understanding is that the sources disagree with each other about how it is used. Three books describe three different regimens, and none of them cites a study establishing any of them. This index does not average them or choose between them, and it does not print amounts on this view — the practitioner view shows each regimen attributed to the source that reported it.

There is no approved product. No regulator anywhere, in anything this index holds, has assessed it for any use.

Before discussing BPC-157 with a clinician, the useful thing to understand is the gap between how much is said about it and how much has been shown in people — and that the gap is not evidence either way. It is a gap.
compound.practitionerSummary:
Synthetic pentadecapeptide, sequence Gly-Glu-Pro-Pro-Pro-Gly-Lys-Pro-Ala-Asp-Asp-Ala-Gly-Leu-Val, MW reported as 1419.556 g/mol, described as a partial sequence of body protection compound isolated from human gastric juice.

Mechanisms reported by the sources held here, all from laboratory work: angiomodulation — described as increasing angiogenesis where needed and decreasing it where not, including in tumour metastasis; nitric oxide stimulation; upregulation of VEGF, FGF and TGF-β; F-actin formation in fibroblasts; increased fibroblast migration and dispersal; increased phosphorylation of paxillin and FAK without change in the amounts produced; upregulation of anti-inflammatory transcription factors and downregulation of TNF-α; upregulation of growth hormone. Additional reported domains: neuroprotection with effects described on serotonergic, dopaminergic, opioid and GABAergic systems; cardioprotection including reported counteraction of neuroleptic-induced QTc prolongation; gastroprotection against ethanol, NSAIDs, corticosteroids, neuroleptics and capsaicin. Topical application reported to accelerate closure after alkali burn via granulation, re-epithelialisation and collagen deposition through ERK1/2.

**Human evidence: none held.** No source in this index reports a clinical trial of BPC-157. Every mechanism and effect above is reported from laboratory or animal work by a practitioner reference, and none of the cited primary papers has been opened by this index.

Pharmacokinetics: nothing. No source held here reports bioavailability, half-life, distribution or elimination for any route.

Routes: subcutaneous and oral are both reported, and one source reports topical in an animal burn model. No source held here compares them, and none reports what fraction of an oral amount is absorbed intact — which for a pentadecapeptide is the question that determines whether an oral route means anything.

Safety, as reported: described as safe in recommended amounts by one source, with caution advised in cancer and other conditions where angiogenesis may need to be suppressed. Rare reactions listed as erythema, transient muscle atrophy, polyarthralgia with hand oedema, and rash. Paediatric safety not established. The angiogenesis caution and the reported anti-tumour effects sit in tension within the same source, and this index records both rather than resolving them.

Regulatory: no approval, no authorisation and no assessment in any jurisdiction, in anything held here.

Protocols: three sources, three different regimens, recorded separately and attributed. None cites a study establishing its amounts.
compound.unknownsSummary: Whether any of this happens in people. This index holds no human trial, no case series, no pharmacokinetic study and no regulatory assessment of BPC-157 — in any jurisdiction, for any use, by any route. The mechanisms recorded here are from laboratory and animal work reported by practitioner references whose own citations have not been traced. Nothing held here establishes an effective amount, a route that delivers intact peptide, a duration, what happens on stopping, what happens with prolonged use, or how the reported pro-angiogenic and anti-tumour effects are reconciled. The volume of discussion around this compound is not evidence, and this record is deliberately arranged so that the two are not mistaken for each other.

compound.molecularDescription: Molecular weight reported as 1419.556 g/mol. The molecular formula printed in the held copy is degraded by optical character recognition and is not transcribed rather than transcribed wrongly.
compound.naturalOrSynthetic: Synthetic. The sources describe it as a partial sequence derived from a protein found in human gastric juice; the peptide administered is made synthetically and is not itself isolated from anyone.
compound.nomenclatureNote: The sources held here describe BPC-157 as 'derived from' body protection compound in gastric juice. That is a statement about where the sequence came from, not a statement that the body produces this fifteen-amino-acid peptide. The inference from 'derived from something the body makes' to 'natural, and therefore safe' is common and is not supported by anything here.

claims.claimText: BPC-157 is a synthetic pentadecapeptide with the sequence Gly-Glu-Pro-Pro-Pro-Gly-Lys-Pro-Ala-Asp-Asp-Ala-Gly-Leu-Val, described by the sources held here as a partial sequence derived from body protection compound found in human gastric juice.
claims.plainLanguageText: BPC-157 is a short chain of fifteen amino acids, made synthetically. Its sequence comes from part of a larger protein found in stomach fluid.
claims.interpretationNotes: Two sources agree on the derivation and one gives the sequence explicitly. This index records the derivation as the sources state it — the sequence is derived from a gastric protein — and does not extend that into a claim that the body produces this peptide, which the sources do not say and which is the inference most often drawn from it.
claims.uncertaintyText: Neither source held here cites an isolation or characterisation paper that this index has read. Whether the administered peptide is identical to any naturally occurring fragment is not established by anything held here.

evidence.interpretation: The source gives the fifteen-residue sequence, the molecular weight, and the category 'gastric pentadecapeptide', and lists Body Protection Compound-157 and Bepecin as other names.
evidence.populationModel: Not applicable — a statement about the molecule.

evidence.interpretation: The source describes BPC-157 as a synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide derived from a peptide called body protecting compound produced in stomach acid.

claims.claimText: The effects attributed to BPC-157 by the sources held here are reported from laboratory and animal studies. No source held by this index reports a clinical trial in humans.
claims.plainLanguageText: Everything these sources say BPC-157 does comes from laboratory and animal work. None of them reports a study in people.
claims.interpretationNotes: This is the load-bearing claim on the record, and it is a claim about the evidence rather than about the compound. Both sources are explicit in their own framing — 'in laboratory studies BPC-157 has been reported to', and 'in several animal studies, and even more anecdotal testimonials from biohackers' — and this index states the consequence plainly rather than leaving a reader to infer it from the absence of a human-evidence section.
claims.uncertaintyText: This is a statement about what this index holds, not about what exists. Human studies of BPC-157 may exist and not be held here; that would be a gap in this register rather than a finding about the compound. What can be said is that nothing supporting a human effect has been extracted, located and recorded here, and that no claim on this page rests on one.

evidence.interpretation: The source introduces its list of effects with 'In laboratory studies BPC-157 has been reported to accelerate the healing of wounds, injuries and tissues', and repeats 'In laboratory studies, BPC-157 is reported' before the detailed list.
evidence.populationModel: Laboratory and animal models, as stated by the source. No human population is described.

evidence.interpretation: The source attributes its list of regenerative effects to 'several animal studies, and even more anecdotal testimonials from biohackers' — placing anecdote alongside animal work as its basis, and naming no human study.
evidence.populationModel: Animal studies and anecdotal report, as stated.

claims.claimText: The healing effects reported in laboratory studies include accelerated wound and tissue healing across tendon, ligament, bone, muscle, skin and gastric mucosa, with reported mechanisms including improved tissue granulation, fibroblast recruitment and collagen formation.
claims.plainLanguageText: In laboratory work, the compound has been reported to speed healing across several tissue types, by encouraging the processes that rebuild tissue.
claims.interpretationNotes: Recorded as a description of what laboratory work has reported, with the tissue list kept as the source gives it rather than generalised to 'healing'. The specific mechanisms named — granulation, fibroblast recruitment, collagen formation — are what the source offers as the how, and are recorded because a mechanism makes a claim checkable in a way that an outcome alone does not.
claims.uncertaintyText: Preclinical, entirely. A result in an animal model is not a result in a person, and a mechanism operating in cell culture is not an effect in a body. The primary papers behind these reports have not been opened by this index, so the models, the doses and the routes used are all unknown here.

evidence.interpretation: The source lists 'Helps heal tissues — promotes microscopic regeneration; improves tissue granulation, fibroblast recruitment and collagen formation' among the effects reported in laboratory studies, with the tissue list given in its opening sentence.
evidence.populationModel: Laboratory studies, models not specified by the source.

evidence.interpretation: The source lists healing of wounds and injuries in muscles, tendons, ligaments, bone and skin, and increased blood flow to damaged areas, as effects consistently observed in animal studies and anecdotal report.

claims.claimText: The sources describe BPC-157 as angiomodulatory rather than simply pro-angiogenic: reported to increase blood vessel formation where needed and decrease it where not, including in tumour metastasis, and to stimulate nitric oxide production and the angiogenic cytokines VEGF, FGF and TGF-β.
claims.plainLanguageText: The sources describe it as adjusting blood vessel growth in both directions rather than only increasing it — including reducing it in the context of tumours.
claims.interpretationNotes: This claim is recorded because of the tension inside it, not despite it. The same source that describes bidirectional angiomodulation and reports inhibition of tumour cell lines also advises caution in cancer and other conditions where angiogenesis may need to be suppressed. Both are recorded, and the tension is recorded as a disagreement on this page rather than resolved by choosing the more reassuring of the two.
claims.uncertaintyText: 'Increased when needed, decreased when needed' is a strong claim and, as stated, an unfalsifiable one: it describes an outcome without a mechanism that would predict which direction occurs when. The source offers no criterion. Nothing held here establishes what determines the direction, or whether the bidirectional behaviour has been observed outside the specific models cited.

evidence.interpretation: The source lists BPC-157 as a 'potent angiomodulatory factor' that 'modulates angiogenesis — increased when needed, decreased when needed such as in tumor metastasis', and separately lists nitric oxide stimulation and the angiogenic cytokines VEGF, FGF and TGF-β.

The source states that despite its ability to promote angiogenesis, BPC-157 is reported to inhibit and counteract increased VEGF expression and subsequent signalling, thus avoiding VEGF-tumorigenesis, and that it inhibits the growth of several tumour cell lines and can counteract tumour cachexia.
evidence.populationModel: Tumour cell lines and laboratory models.

evidence.interpretation: The same source advises using BPC-157 with caution in cancer and other conditions where angiogenesis may need to be suppressed — a caution that sits against its own account of bidirectional angiomodulation and anti-tumour effect.

claims.claimText: The sources held here report both subcutaneous and oral administration, and topical application in an animal burn model, without comparing them or reporting bioavailability for any route.
claims.plainLanguageText: Injection under the skin, swallowing, and application to the skin are all described. No source held here says how much reaches the body by any of these routes, or compares them.
claims.interpretationNotes: Recorded as a claim because the oral route is the one a reader is most likely to act on and the one the sources support least. A fifteen-residue peptide taken orally faces gastric and intestinal proteolysis, and whether any survives intact is precisely the question the sources do not address. This index records that they report the route and records that they establish nothing about it.
claims.uncertaintyText: No bioavailability figure, no pharmacokinetic study, and no comparison between routes appears in anything held here. That an amount is reported for a route is not evidence that the route delivers the peptide. For the oral route in particular, this index holds nothing addressing whether the peptide survives digestion.

evidence.interpretation: The source gives separate subcutaneous and oral amounts under 'Dosage', and lists an available injectable solution strength. It gives no bioavailability figure for either.

The source reports that topical treatment accelerated wound closure following an alkali burn, with a mechanism attributed to granulation, re-epithelialisation, dermal remodelling and collagen deposition through ERK1/2 signalling.
evidence.populationModel: Animal burn model; species not specified by the source.

claims.claimText: The sources held here report no approved product, no regulatory assessment and no approved indication for BPC-157 in any jurisdiction.
claims.plainLanguageText: There is no approved medicine containing BPC-157. No regulator, in anything this index holds, has assessed it for any use.
claims.interpretationNotes: Recorded as an explicit claim rather than as an empty regulatory section, because an empty section reads as 'not yet filled in' and this is a finding. Two of the three sources are practitioner handbooks that name brand names and manufacturers for other compounds — including for tesamorelin in the same volume — and name none here.
claims.uncertaintyText: This is a statement about what the sources held here record. It is not a statement about the regulatory position in any particular jurisdiction, which would require a regulatory source, and this index holds none for this compound. Regulatory status also changes, and the most recent source here is from 2025.

evidence.interpretation: The source's 'Other Name(s)' field for BPC-157 lists only descriptive names and Bepecin, with no brand name, manufacturer or approval — in contrast with the same handbook's tesamorelin entry, which names Egrifta and Theratechnologies.

claims.claimText: Reported adverse effects are limited: one source describes BPC-157 as safe in recommended amounts, listing erythema, transient muscle atrophy, polyarthralgia with hand oedema and rash as rare reactions, and states that paediatric safety has not been established.
claims.plainLanguageText: The handbook describes it as safe at the amounts it recommends and lists a small number of uncommon reactions. It states that safety in children has not been established.
claims.interpretationNotes: Recorded with its provenance foremost. 'Reported safe in recommended dosages' is a statement by a practitioner handbook about amounts that the same handbook recommends, with no study cited for either the amounts or the safety. A short list of adverse effects is what one expects when there is no systematic collection of them, and absence of reported harm is not evidence of safety.
claims.uncertaintyText: No human safety study, no pharmacovigilance record and no systematic adverse-event collection appears in anything this index holds. A compound with no trials has no trial safety data, and a short adverse-effect list from a handbook is not the same thing. Nothing here addresses prolonged use, interactions, or use in any specific population.

evidence.interpretation: The source states that BPC-157 is reported safe in recommended dosages, advises caution in cancer and conditions where angiogenesis may need suppressing, and notes that redness and pain at the injection site may occur.
The source lists rare adverse reactions as erythema, transient muscle atrophy, polyarthralgia combined with hand oedema, and rash, and states that safety in paediatrics has not been established.

notYetSupported.statement: That BPC-157 produces any effect in humans.
notYetSupported.why: This index holds no clinical trial, no case series and no case report for BPC-157. Every source held here reports laboratory or animal work, or anecdote, and says so in its own words.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: A clinical trial publication, or a case series with defined outcomes, obtained and extracted with locators.

notYetSupported.statement: What proportion of an orally administered amount reaches the circulation intact.
notYetSupported.why: Two sources report an oral amount and neither reports a bioavailability figure or a pharmacokinetic study. For a fifteen-residue peptide this is the question that determines whether an oral route delivers anything at all, and nothing held here addresses it.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: A pharmacokinetic study comparing oral and parenteral administration, in any species, reporting plasma concentrations of intact peptide.

notYetSupported.statement: An effective amount, frequency or duration for any purpose.
notYetSupported.why: Three sources give three different regimens and none cites a study establishing any of them. This index does not average regimens and does not choose between sources, so it has no amount to state.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: A dose-finding study, or any source that states the basis for the amounts it recommends.

notYetSupported.statement: The safety profile of BPC-157 in humans, including with prolonged use.
notYetSupported.why: No human safety study, pharmacovigilance record or systematic adverse-event collection is held here. The adverse effects recorded on this page are a short list from one practitioner handbook, which is not a safety dataset.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: Human safety data from a trial or a registry.

notYetSupported.statement: Whether the reported pro-angiogenic and anti-tumour effects can both be true, and what determines which occurs.
notYetSupported.why: One source reports bidirectional angiomodulation and inhibition of tumour cell lines, and in the same entry advises caution in cancer. This index records the tension rather than resolving it, because resolving it would require the primary literature it does not hold.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: The primary papers behind both claims, read closely enough to establish the models and the conditions under which each direction was observed.

notYetSupported.statement: The regulatory position of BPC-157 in any named jurisdiction.
notYetSupported.why: No source held here is a regulatory source. The absence of a named product in three practitioner handbooks is consistent with there being no approval, and it is not the same as having checked with a regulator.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: A statement from a named authority in a named jurisdiction, with a date.

notYetSupported.statement: What the laboratory studies behind every mechanism on this page actually did and found.
notYetSupported.why: Both practitioner sources cite their primary literature by superscript or by a link to the author's own website. None of those citations has been obtained or opened by this index.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: The primary publications, obtained and read, with each mechanism checked against the paper reporting it.

routes.limitationsNotes: Reported by a practitioner handbook as the route it recommends. No pharmacokinetic data, no bioavailability figure and no study establishing this route appear in anything held here. Recording a route is not a statement that it is appropriate, effective or safe.

The source gives an oral amount and nothing else. Whether a fifteen-residue peptide survives gastric and intestinal proteolysis in any useful proportion is the question this route turns on, and no source held here addresses it. The oral route is recorded here because a source reports it, and it is the least supported route on this record.

protocols.safetyNotes: The source states BPC-157 is reported safe in recommended dosages, and notes injection-site redness and pain.

disagreements.topic: How much BPC-157, and how often: three sources describe three different subcutaneous regimens for overlapping purposes.
disagreements.plainLanguageText: Three books describe three different regimens for the same compound, and none of them says what that is based on. This index shows each one attributed to the book that reported it rather than combining them into a single figure.
disagreements.explanationNotes: The differences are not obviously explained by population, route or formulation, because none of the three sources specifies a population and two do not specify a formulation. What distinguishes them is the framing: one is a clinical handbook, one a consumer book citing its own website, one a set of worked personas. The most economical explanation is that no source is working from a dose-finding study, because this index holds no evidence that one exists.
disagreements.resolutionRequirement: A dose-finding study in any species, or any source that states the basis for the amount it recommends. Absent either, this index will continue to show three attributed regimens and no recommended amount.

positions.positionText: The Peptide Handbook gives 300-600 mcg subcutaneously daily for 30 days for general use, and 300-500 mcg twice daily where the use is injury-specific.
Optimize Your Health with Therapeutic Peptides gives a single recommended amount: 250 mcg injected subcutaneously twice a day.

The Complete Guide to Peptides uses 500 mcg daily in its joint and tissue repair example, and 250 mcg twice daily in its skin repair example — two different amounts within the same book, for different stated purposes.

disagreements.topic: Whether BPC-157 should be avoided in cancer, or may be protective against it.
disagreements.plainLanguageText: One handbook says to use caution in cancer because the compound affects blood vessel growth, and the same handbook reports that it inhibits tumour growth in laboratory studies. Both statements are on the record, and this index does not choose between them.
disagreements.explanationNotes: Both positions come from the same source, which makes this a disagreement within a source rather than between sources — and arguably the more instructive kind. A compound described as increasing blood vessel formation where needed and decreasing it where not is described in terms that cannot be wrong, and the clinical caution attached to it suggests the author does not fully rely on that description either. This index records the caution and the reported anti-tumour effect side by side, and treats neither as settling the question.
disagreements.resolutionRequirement: The primary literature behind the anti-tumour reports, read closely enough to establish the models and conditions; and any clinical evidence, of which this index holds none.

positions.positionText: The source advises that although BPC-157 is angiomodulatory, it should be used with caution in cancer and other conditions where angiogenesis may need to be suppressed.

The same source reports that BPC-157 inhibits and counteracts increased VEGF expression, thus avoiding VEGF-tumorigenesis, inhibits the growth of several tumour cell lines, and can counteract tumour cachexia.

regulatory.indicationContext: No approved indication is recorded by any source held here.
regulatory.authority: None. No source held by this index is a regulatory source for BPC-157, and none names an approving authority.
regulatory.notes: Recorded as 'not approved' on the basis that three practitioner handbooks — two of which name brand names and manufacturers for other compounds, including in the same volume — record none for BPC-157. That is consistent with there being no approval anywhere; it is not the same as a regulator having said so. This index holds no regulatory document for this compound and cannot state the position in any named jurisdiction. The date is the date the sources were read.
